query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An ab initio free‐energy method based on DFT that employs thermodynamic integration in a two‐phase coexistence simulation can accurately calculate melting properties—namely, the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and the volume change at the melting point—in high‐melting refractory materials.
generation.material_initial_state: A crystalline, high‐melting refractory material in its solid phase at ambient or moderate temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a DFT-based ab initio free-energy approach using thermodynamic integration along with two-phase (solid/liquid) molecular dynamics simulations.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted near the expected melting temperature under controlled temperature and volume conditions, ensuring both solid and liquid phases are properly sampled.
generation.structural_mediator: The free-energy difference between the solid and liquid phases as computed through the thermodynamic integration scheme.
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic integration tracks the gradual change in free energy between the solid and liquid states. This allows for the extraction of the melting temperature when the free energies match, along with derivation of associated entropy and enthalpy changes and volume differences at the transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to yield melting properties that are in close agreement with experimental values or high-accuracy benchmarks when DFT parameters are appropriately chosen, despite the high simulation cost.
generation.baseline: Conventional experimental measurements of melting properties which are challenging due to high melting temperatures.
generation.boundary: The method is constrained by its high computational expense and sensitivity to the DFT exchange-correlation functional and simulation parameters; uncertainties in these choices may impact absolute values while trends should remain reliable.
generation.uncertainty: The precise numerical agreement of melting properties with experiment may vary due to DFT approximations and simulation setup, but the method should still reliably capture the key trends and relative differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of DFT-based ab initio molecular dynamics simulations using thermodynamic integration in a two-phase coexistence setup to compute free energy differences between the solid and liquid phases for a refractory material. Extract the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting, then compare these computed values with available experimental measurements.
measurements: Volume change at the melting point
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the computed melting temperature and fusion properties consistently deviate from experimental or high-trust benchmark values beyond expected error margins (considering DFT approximations), then the hypothesis that the ab initio free-energy method can accurately predict these properties will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
